The University of Paris, the University of Oxford, the University of Bologna — all were founded under ecclesiastical authority in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The monks and clerics who populated these institutions were not enemies of learning. They were its custodians.

The list of scientists who were devout Christians is not a list of exceptions. It is a catalog of the founders of modern science. Copernicus was a Catholic canon. Galileo remained a Catholic throughout his life. Johannes Kepler described his astronomical work as "thinking God's thoughts after him." Isaac Newton wrote more pages of theology than of physics. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Georges Lemaitre, who proposed the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. The assumption that scientific genius and religious belief are incompatible is contradicted by the very history of science itself.

The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued in *Science and the Modern World* (1925) that modern science was made possible by the medieval conviction, rooted in Christian theology, that the universe is rational and ordered — that it operates according to consistent laws because it is the creation of a rational God. This conviction, Whitehead argued, provided the philosophical foundation for the scientific method: the belief that the universe is intelligible, that its patterns can be discovered, and that the human mind is equipped to discover them. Without this conviction, the enterprise of science would have no warrant.

## Scientists Who Believe

The claim that serious scientists cannot be serious believers is refuted by the existence of serious scientists who are serious believers. Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the National Institutes of Health, is an evangelical Christian who has written extensively about the compatibility of faith and science. John Polkinghorne, a Cambridge particle physicist who became an Anglican priest, developed a sophisticated theology of science that integrates quantum mechanics and trinitarian theology. Jennifer Wiseman, a senior astrophysicist at NASA, has spoken publicly about how her study of the cosmos deepens rather than diminishes her Christian faith.

A 2009 Pew Research Center survey found that 51 percent of scientists believe in God or a higher power. The number is lower than the general population, but it is not negligible — and it demolishes the claim that scientific expertise is incompatible with religious belief. The National Academy of Sciences includes members who are devout Christians, Jews, Muslims, and adherents of other traditions. They do not check their faith at the laboratory door.

## Models for the Relationship

If science and faith are not at war, what is their relationship? Several models have been proposed, each with strengths and limitations.

Stephen Jay Gould proposed the NOMA model — Non-Overlapping Magisteria — in his 1999 book *Rocks of Ages*. On this view, science and religion address fundamentally different questions: science asks how the natural world works; religion asks what it means and how we should live. The two domains do not overlap, and conflict arises only when one trespasses on the other's territory. The NOMA model has the virtue of clarity, but many thinkers — both scientific and theological — find it too neat. If God created the universe, then God's creative action must have some relationship to the universe that science studies. And if science discovers features of the universe that bear on questions of meaning — the fine-tuning of cosmological constants, the emergence of consciousness — then the magisteria do overlap, whether we want them to or not.

The dialogue model, associated with Ian Barbour and others, holds that science and religion address different questions but that their answers interact and can inform each other. Scientific discoveries about the age of the universe, the evolution of life, and the nature of consciousness raise questions that theology has resources to address. Theological convictions about the goodness of creation, the value of human life, and the reality of moral obligation raise questions that science alone cannot answer. The two disciplines are in conversation, not competition.

The integration model goes further, arguing that science and theology can be woven into a single, coherent framework. Teilhard de Chardin, the Jesuit paleontologist, attempted a grand synthesis of evolutionary biology and Christian theology. More recently, scholars associated with the John Templeton Foundation have pursued research at the intersection of science and religion, exploring questions about the nature of consciousness, the fine-tuning of the cosmos, and the evolutionary origins of altruism.

No single model captures the full complexity of the relationship. What all serious models share is the rejection of the warfare metaphor — the recognition that science and faith, whatever their tensions, are not enemies but neighbors, occupying adjacent rooms in the house of human inquiry, and that the conversation between them is one of the most important conversations a thoughtful person can have.

## The Questions Science Cannot Answer

The limits of science are not weaknesses. They are the boundaries of a discipline that has defined its domain with admirable precision. Science investigates the natural world through observation, hypothesis, experimentation, and revision. It does this extraordinarily well. But there are questions that the scientific method, by its own design, is not equipped to answer. Why is there something rather than nothing? What grounds moral obligation? Does life have purpose? Is the universe meaningful, or is meaning a human projection onto an indifferent cosmos? What happens when we die?

These are not failed scientific questions waiting for better instruments. They are philosophical and theological questions that require different tools — tools that include reason, tradition, experience, revelation, and the cumulative wisdom of communities that have wrestled with these questions for millennia. The scientist who says "science cannot answer that question" is not confessing a limitation. The scientist is defining a boundary. And the theologian who says "let me bring a different set of tools to the table" is not trespassing on science's territory. The theologian is working in an adjacent field where the soil is different and the methods must be different too.

The deepest mistake of the new atheism — the movement associated with Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Christopher Hitchens, and Daniel Dennett — was not its criticism of religion's failures, much of which was deserved. The deepest mistake was its claim that science could replace religion — that empirical investigation could answer every meaningful human question, and that any question science could not answer was therefore not a real question. This is not a scientific claim. It is a philosophical claim — the claim known as scientism — and it is a claim that most philosophers, including many who are atheists, regard as unjustified. Science is magnificent at telling us how the universe works. It has nothing to say about whether the universe matters.

The war between science and faith is not a war that needs to be won. It is a war that never existed — except in the imagination of polemicists on both sides who found it more useful to fight than to think. The actual history is richer, messier, and more hopeful than the myth. And the sooner we leave the myth behind, the sooner we can get on with the real work: asking the deepest questions about the universe with every tool we have — including both the telescope and the prayer.

chapters.title: The Trinity Is Not Optional
chapters.summary: We treat the Trinity as the church's embarrassing arithmetic. It is the most practical claim Christianity makes, and the ground everyone is standing on.
chapters.body:
A child asks how God can be three and also one, and the adults at the table change the subject. We have made the Trinity the church's embarrassing arithmetic, the doctrine we recite in the creed on Sunday and never once use on Monday, the freight we haul because the councils told us to. We can explain why the cross matters and why grace matters and why prayer matters. Ask most believers why it matters that God is triune and you will get a long pause and a diagram involving water or an egg.

This is exactly backward. The doctrine no one uses is the ground everyone is standing on.

Give the skeptic the full force of the objection first, because it is a serious one. The word Trinity is not in the Bible. The fully developed doctrine was hammered out over three centuries and finalized at councils that emperors convened, beginning with Nicaea in the year 325, summoned by Constantine, who cared at least as much about imperial unity as about theology. The fights were political and often ugly. Athanasius, the doctrine's great defender, was driven into exile five times. And on its face the claim looks like incoherence, one equals three, or like later Greek philosophy bolted onto the plain monotheism of a Jewish prophet who only ever told people to worship the God of Israel. Stated that way, the suspicion is understandable. A reasonable person could conclude the church invented a riddle and then demanded everyone affirm it.

Grant the mess. The councils were human and the politics were real. But the doctrine was not an imposition laid on top of the New Testament. It was a synthesis forced out from underneath it, the church's refusal to drop any of the things the text would not let it drop.

The first Christians were Jews. They said the Shema every day, hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, and they meant it with their lives, and they died rather than grant that Caesar was a god. And these same fierce monotheists prayed to Jesus, sang to him as Lord, baptized in the threefold name, and described the Spirit as God present and personal among them. They did not arrive at the Trinity by speculation. They were driven to it by the refusal to let go of four things all at once. The Father is God. Jesus is worshipped as God. The Spirit is God. There is one God. Arius, in the fourth century, offered a clean way out. Make the Son a high and glorious creature, the first and best thing God made, but a creature, not God himself. It solved the math. The church looked at the solution and saw that it dissolved the gospel, because a creature cannot save, and a Savior you worship who is less than God is an idol however exalted. At Nicaea the church answered Arius with a single word that is not elegant and was never meant to be, homoousios, of the same being as the Father. Athanasius spent his whole hunted life on that one word because he saw what it was protecting (Athanasius 2011).

What it was protecting is most visible not in a creed but in a prayer. On the night before he died, in the seventeenth chapter of John, Jesus prays aloud, and the prayer opens a window into the inside of God. He speaks to the Father of a glory the two of them shared before the world existed. He speaks of being loved by the Father before the foundation of the world. And he prays that his people would be brought inside that very love, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you (John 17:21-24 ESV). The doctrine of the Trinity is, in the end, only the church learning to say what that prayer takes for granted. Before there was a universe to love, there was love. The Father loved the Son. The love did not begin when creatures arrived to receive it.

This is the thing the doctrine secures, and everything turns on it. Love is not something God started doing when he made a world. Love is what God is, eternally, in himself, three persons giving and receiving without beginning and without end. The Greek fathers had a word for the way the persons make room for one another in this endless mutual life, perichoresis, a kind of eternal indwelling. Augustine spent fifteen books circling it, finally finding its trace in the structure of love itself, which always requires a lover, a beloved, and the love that passes between them (Augustine 1991). C. S. Lewis, trying to get ordinary readers to feel it, said that God is not a static thing but a dynamic, pulsating activity, a life, almost a kind of dance (Lewis 1952).

Now the reversal, the thing the bored Sunday believer never expects. This is the most practical claim Christianity makes. Imagine the alternative were true, that God is a single solitary power, a lonely monad on the throne of the universe. Then God needed the world in order to have anything to love, which means love is something God takes up, a later activity, and the most basic thing about ultimate reality is not love but sheer undifferentiated power and will. A universe with a unitarian god at the top is a universe in which force is more fundamental than love, and the self that images that god will believe, all the way down, that power is what finally matters and relationship is what you do once power is secured. But if God is triune, then the deepest fact about all that exists is not force and not the lonely will. It is self-giving love between persons, older than time. Catherine LaCugna argued that this is the entire point, that the doctrine is not abstract at all but tells us reality itself is personal and relational at its root (LaCugna 1991).

That detonates the central myth of the modern self. Charles Taylor describes the self the Enlightenment built as buffered and sovereign, the individual who imagines he is most free when he owes nothing to anyone and answers to no one he did not choose (Taylor 2007). The Trinity says the opposite is the truth of things. You were made in the image of a God who is community, whose very being is gift, and so you become most yourself not by self-possession but by self-donation, not by guarding your life but by giving it away. The lonely autonomous self is not the height of freedom. It is a small imitation of the lonely god who does not exist.

And the cross is the Trinity made visible in time. On Golgotha the Son gives himself, the Father gives the Son, the Spirit holds them across the dark. Strip out the Trinity and the cross becomes a horror, one being punishing another being to satisfy his anger, which is the caricature the critics rightly despise. Hold the Trinity and the cross is God giving himself, the eternal self-gift of Father, Son, and Spirit reaching into history and going all the way down into death and out the other side. Karl Barth insisted that God's very being is this act, that God is the one who loves in freedom, and that what happened on the cross was not foreign to God but the truest revelation of who God has always been (Barth 1957).

I will confess that I have treated this doctrine as a museum piece, something to defend against heretics rather than something to live inside. I have preached a God of love on Sunday and then spent the week ordering my life as though the basic structure of reality were competition and self-protection, getting mine, securing my position, keeping score. That is functional unitarianism. It is the practical worship of a single solitary power, whatever I say in the creed. The way a man guards his own life gives away the god he actually believes in, and mine has too often been the lonely one.

The child's question was the right question, and changing the subject was the failure. How can God be three and one. The answer is that God is love, and love has never been able to exist alone, because love requires one who loves and one who is loved and the love itself that binds them, and so the God who is love has never once been solitary, and was never going to make us to be solitary either. He made us to be brought inside the oldest love there is. The doctrine you thought was useless is the reason you exist and the home you are being called into. That is not arithmetic. That is the whole thing.

### Works Cited
